args.note: I've written analysis.md. Verdicts: Young Americans Center partly, Bill Reynolds yes, smells like school no, school pages 3 (pages 20, 42 and 50). The book does not cross the stakeholders' line. Its villains are a crony House and an emergency power with no expiry, and the ending refuses both the debt wipe-out and central power. Inez and Morrow & Sons are the honest businesses, and the debt gets paid down. Main risks: 1) The surface reads as a progressive dystopia, especially to anyone who reads only Issue 01. 2) A gambler's debt passing to his son by law is not how real credit works, which matters to a partner that runs a real bank. 3) Issue 03's bands and lever (p41-50) are too opaque for a first read. 4) Every character speaks in the same clipped one-liners, which this AI-skeptical audience will notice. 5) Ada's name is not spoken until p38, and the p18 "full-page splash" sits on a page with three other panels. B11 behaves like Bill but doesn't sound like him: he never tells a story and nothing about him is Western.
